name: Morphine
summary: The reference opioid, and a useful lesson in why blood levels can mislead. Morphine is water-soluble, so unlike most drugs here it crosses into the brain slowly — the effect peaks well after the blood level does. Dosing again because it 'is not working yet' is how people overshoot it.
mechanism: Full agonist at mu-opioid receptors. Analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression and constipation all come from the same receptor in different places, which is why they cannot be separated by dose. Respiratory depression is the fatal one: the brainstem simply stops responding to rising carbon dioxide.

oral.note: Three quarters is removed on the first pass through the liver, which is why oral doses are several times larger than injected ones for the same effect. Much of what is lost becomes M6G, which is itself active — so the oral route is relatively more M6G-driven.

iv.note: Complete, but note the effect-site lag: peak brain effect comes 15-30 minutes after the blood peak because morphine crosses the blood-brain barrier slowly.

oral_mr.note: Modified-release tablets, designed for a flat 12-hour profile. Crushing one destroys the mechanism and delivers the entire 12-hour supply at once — a frequent and sometimes fatal error.

pathways.name: Morphine-3-glucuronide
pathways.note: The largest product. No opioid activity, but neuroexcitatory — associated with the agitation, twitching and hyperalgesia seen at high doses or in renal impairment.

pathways.name: Morphine-6-glucuronide
pathways.note: More potent than morphine itself and cleared entirely by the kidneys. In renal impairment it accumulates over days, producing deepening sedation and respiratory depression that appears long after the dose — a classic delayed overdose.

effect_levels.label: 30 µg/L — effective analgesia in most patients
100 µg/L — respiratory depression in the non-tolerant

risk: Switch the cursor between the blood curve and the effect curve and note the gap. The effect is still climbing for 15-30 minutes after the blood level has peaked, and that gap is where accidental double-dosing happens.
Kidney function matters more here than liver function, because the active metabolite M6G is renally cleared. In renal impairment, repeated ordinary doses accumulate into an overdose over days.
Tolerance to euphoria and analgesia develops much faster than tolerance to respiratory depression, so escalating to recover the effect narrows the safety margin with every step.
Any other depressant — alcohol, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids — multiplies the respiratory risk. See interactions.
Modified-release tablets must never be crushed or chewed.
